title: Ohtani’s Slump Unveiled: Can He Recover in Time for a Comeback?
body:
Shohei Ohtani is slated to start for the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3 of the World Series on Wednesday, manager Dave Roberts confirmed on Thursday. The announcement, which required a formal statement at all, underscores how dramatically the two‑time MVP’s performance has dipped in the postseason. After a season in which Ohtani dazzled with 44 home runs, 100 RBIs and a 2.98 ERA as a pitcher, the Japanese star has struggled to find his rhythm, prompting a flurry of speculation about the root causes and whether there is enough time to reverse the trend before the series heads into a decisive Game 5, if necessary.

The slump is not merely a statistical blip. In his first two World Series appearances, Ohtani posted a combined .267 batting average with three homers and five RBIs, but this year’s numbers tell a different story. Over his first four postseason outings, he has gone 4‑for‑26 at the plate, a .154 average, and has recorded just one strikeout in 13 innings pitched, with an ERA hovering above 6.00. The contrast to his regular‑season dominance is stark, and it has forced the Dodgers’ front office to reassess how to best utilize a player who is simultaneously a premier hitter and a frontline starter.

Analysts point to a confluence of factors that may be feeding Ohtani’s downturn. First, the cumulative toll of a 162‑game schedule combined with the added strain of pitching every fifth day appears to be eroding his stamina. Unlike most two‑way players, Ohtani shoulders both the physical demands of a starting rotation and the daily grind of a middle‑of‑the‑order bat. The Dodgers’ medical staff has noted minor fatigue in his lower back and a lingering shoulder tightness that, while not severe enough to sideline him, could be affecting his swing mechanics and pitch command. Second, the heightened scrutiny of World Series pitching—where opponents study every nuance—has left Ohtani with fewer “good” pitches to rely on, forcing him to swing at marginal offerings and resulting in a higher strikeout rate. Finally, the psychological pressure of living up to the “Greatest Player in the World” narrative may be amplifying every misstep, a burden that even seasoned veterans find hard to shake.

Roberts’ decision to keep Ohtani in the lineup signals confidence that the pitcher‑hitter can still be a game‑changer, but it also reflects a pragmatic acknowledgment of limited alternatives. Los Angeles’ bench depth is solid, yet the team lacks another left‑handed power bat with Ohtani’s on‑base skills. In the bullpen, the Dodgers have relied heavily on their closer, yet the series has already seen a surge in high‑leverage situations that demand a starter who can also contribute offensively. By slotting Ohtani into the lineup, Roberts is betting that a few adjustments—perhaps a shortened pitching stint, a more patient approach at the plate, or a slight tweak in his pre‑game routine—could spark a resurgence.

The Dodgers’ coaching staff has already hinted at possible tweaks. Pitching coach Josh Baker suggested a modest reduction in Ohtani’s pitch count for the upcoming start, aiming to preserve his arm for a potential Game 5 while still giving him a chance to impact the game early. Hitting coach Brant Brown, meanwhile, is reportedly working with Ohtani on a more selective swing path, emphasizing contact over power to rebuild confidence. If the adjustments bear fruit, Ohtani could provide the spark the Dodgers need to swing momentum back in their favor.

Looking ahead, the series hangs in a delicate balance. The Dodgers trail 2‑1, and the next two games will likely determine whether Los Angeles can force a decisive fifth contest. Ohtani’s performance will be a barometer for the team’s overall health; a bounce‑back could galvanize the roster, while continued struggles might expose deeper fatigue issues that could linger into the offseason. For now, fans and pundits alike will be watching closely as the two‑way star steps onto the mound and into the batter’s box, hoping that the roots of his slump can be pruned before the championship slips away.
